chunks.section: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
chunks.text: Minuk Ma Kaiyun Guo Jiarui Ding Affiliation: University of British Columbia Affiliation: {minukma, gky0722}@cs.ubc.ca , jiarui.ding@ubc.ca

Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scicuratebench-D885/ .

Modern scientific research increasingly begins with dataset curation, systematically gathering experimental data from published literature that satisfy precise criteria. This is especially common in life sciences research to build atlases by merging multiple similar experimental data Liu et al. (2022) ; Chu et al. (2023) ; Xu et al. (2024) ; Xue et al. (2025) ; Youngblut et al. (2026) . For example, researchers may seek "all publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from cancer patients with associated immunotherapy response outcomes". This seemingly straightforward task is extraordinarily time-consuming in practice. Scientific papers are long, with extensive supplementary materials, and critical information may be embedded in externally hosted data (e.g., GEO Edgar et al. (2002) or Mendeley Data Mendeley Data (2016) ). Researchers must verify multiple conditions simultaneously: the correct assay type (scRNA-seq, not bulk RNA-seq), disease context (cancer), clinical information (treatment outcomes), and crucially, that data are newly generated (not reanalyzed from prior work) and publicly available. A single paper might report multiple experiments, and only one of them may meet all criteria. While modern search engines allow for the identification of potentially relevant papers, the challenge lies in verifying whether each paper precisely satisfies all the conditions in the query. This precision requirement, combined with the length and heterogeneity of scientific documents, makes automated curation still far from being satisfactorily solved.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) Brown et al. (2020) ; OpenAI (2023) ; Anthropic (2024) ; Chowdhery et al. (2023) have shown promise for literature search tasks. Powerful models such as GPT-4o OpenAI (2023) have demonstrated effectiveness in re-ranking candidate documents Sun et al. (2023) and identifying citations for specific claims Press et al. (2024) . However, existing literature search benchmarks focus on broad relevance ranking or single-claim attribution rather than confirming that papers precisely meet multiple conjunctive experimental criteria. Also, most of them do not include supplementary files or hosted data as search targets, deviating from practical needs. To address this gap, we introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark comprising 200 expert-annotated papers from mainstream scientific journals, with the goal of facilitating research in realistic scientific data curation. The benchmark includes two tasks that mirror real-world workflows: Science Paper Classification, which requires determining whether experiments meet specified criteria, and Structured Information Retrieval, which involves extracting experimental metadata from papers that satisfy the search conditions.

We show that popular LLM reasoning methods achieve only suboptimal performance on the benchmark. To further push performance and study the factors contributing to success, we propose LangPoli, a multi-agent framework that adaptively creates tools to retrieve information from heterogeneous documents and verify precise conditions in the query. Unlike code-action agents that couple planning and implementation in a single generation step, LangPoli separates a natural-language policy from environment-specific code synthesis. This enables the creation of dynamic tools tailored to each document’s unique structure. Actor agents then convert these verbal action guidelines into executable code to collect observations. A critic agent evaluates the accumulated evidence against the query predicates and provides info-gap feedback to the policy agent, creating a closed loop that enables self-improvement over iterations. We note that concepts such as the plan/action structure Wan et al. (2024) ; Erdogan et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) , code as action instead of predefined sets Wang et al. (2024b) ; Yuan et al. (2024) ; Wölflein et al. (2025) ; Nguyen et al. (2025) , evaluation using LLM agents Shinn et al. (2023) ; Miao et al. (2024) ; Zhuge et al. (2025) ; Yuan and Xie (2025) , and adaptive tool usage Schick et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Wang et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2025) have been established in the field, and LangPoli is a domain-specific adaptation of these components for the underexplored task of scientific data curation. Still, benchmarking LangPoli and other methods on SciCurateBench reveals the difficulty of the task and provides insights into the factors contributing to success.

Figure 1: SciCurateBench promotes adaptive tool creation for efficiently exploring, analyzing, and summarizing heterogeneous scientific files, including manuscripts, supplementary data, and raw datasets. We provide comprehensive benchmarking of popular agentic AI baselines on scientific data curation, including plain LLMs, reasoning agents, tool-using agents, tool-creating agents, and feedback-based agents. Our experiments show that LangPoli is the only method that performs consistently well on both tasks of SciCurateBench, reaching 83.16% F1 on paper classification (vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and 69.43% F1 on structured information retrieval (vs. 59.13% for the strongest baseline). The framework also shows strong performance on public benchmarks of LitSearch Ajith et al. (2024) , BEIR Thakur et al. (2021) , and TREC Craswell et al. (2020) , particularly excelling on long documents where its created tools enable efficient targeted exploration. We show that the tools generated by LangPoli maintain high execution success rates and code maintainability scores while effectively supporting the exploration process. Finally, we explore curriculum transfer, a form of knowledge distillation where successful tool creation sequences are refactored and transferred as structured curricula to accelerate performance on related tasks. This approach enables the system to leverage problem-solving strategies learned from previous curation tasks, further improving efficiency and effectiveness on new scientific data curation problems.

Scientific literature search and curation. The challenge of finding and processing scientific literature has driven the development of research assistance systems. Classical retrieval models such as BM25 Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) , a term-based ranking method derived from the probabilistic relevance framework, remain a strong baseline. Information-retrieval benchmarks such as BEIR Thakur et al. (2021) , TREC Craswell et al. (2020) , and MTEB Muennighoff et al. (2023) have facilitated research on literature search by evaluating across various domains and query types. As more targeted research, LitSearch Ajith et al. (2024) simulates literature search from machine learning papers. However, these benchmarks primarily assess candidate ranking by broad relevance to user queries. Recent papers applied LLMs to retrieve relevant documents or data, and standardize He et al. (2025) ; Su et al. (2025) ; Cui et al. (2025) ; Alyafeai et al. (2025) ; Asai et al. (2026) . CiteME Press et al. (2024) evaluates whether LLM agents can identify which paper a text excerpt references, targeting citation attribution for fact-checking. While RankGPT Sun et al. (2023) and CiteME have benchmarked GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 on re-ranking and citation tasks, evaluation of other agentic AI families remains unexplored. An extended discussion is provided in Appendix A . In contrast to previous works, our SciCurateBench addresses a different yet practical bottleneck of experimental data curation. While researchers can gather top candidates using search engines, verifying whether each candidate actually published the desired experimental data (e.g., "published data using technique X with metric Y and metadata Z") poses additional layers of grounding, verification, and cross-checking challenges.

LLM reasoning and tool creation. Recent advances have enhanced LLM reasoning through structured prompting Wei et al. (2022) , tool integration Cai et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2024b) ; Yuan et al. (2024) ; Wölflein et al. (2025) , and feedback-based refinement Shinn et al. (2023) ; Zhuge et al. (2025) ; Yuan and Xie (2025) . LangPoli is structurally close to these methods but decouples policy (guidelines) from environment-specific implementation (code). Retrieval-augmented LLMs Wang et al. (2025b) ; Jin et al. (2025) ground claims with evidence from web-based Li et al. (2025c) ; Li et al. (2025d) or static corpus Gutiérrez et al. (2025) ; Asai et al. (2026) . As the field is rapidly evolving, we point the readers to a recent survey Singh et al. (2026) for more related methods. In this work, we focus our scope on scientific data curation and select baselines that are widely acknowledged, rather than extensive lists of agentic coders. Scientific AI agents. Recent works have begun applying LLM agents to scientific workflows Chen et al. (2024) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Mitchener et al. (2025) ; M. Bran et al. (2024) ; Lu et al. (2026) ; Gottweis et al. (2026) ; Xiao et al. (2026) . Existing research on scientific AI agents predominantly targets downstream tasks of hypothesis generation, experimental design, data analysis, or model fitting, and assumes that curated input data is already available. By contrast, the upstream bottleneck of curating experimental data from raw, heterogeneous primary literature remains underexplored. SciCurateBench and LangPoli target this upstream gap, and we expect strong synergy with existing research on scientific AI agent.
We introduce SciCurateBench , a benchmark designed to evaluate AI systems on realistic data curation tasks.

Paper Selection. As shown in Figure 1 , we curated 200 papers from major life science journals ( Nature , Cell , Science , etc.; 2016–2025) focusing on two query types reflecting realistic workflows: (1) scRNA-seq with immunotherapy response: identifying newly generated single-cell RNA sequencing data from cancer patients with associated clinical outcomes, and (2) paired scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq: identifying papers with simultaneously profiled transcriptomic and T-cell receptor sequences across disease conditions. Papers were identified through PubMed searches using domain-specific keywords (“single-cell RNA sequencing,” “scTCR-seq,” “immunotherapy response,” “checkpoint blockade”) and expert-curated paper lists from atlas construction projects Xue et al. (2025) . Annotation Protocol. Three domain experts with a life science background (3–12 years experience) performed annotation by examining full manuscripts, supplementary materials, and hosted data. Annotations were conducted in two stages: primary annotation (160 hours) followed by independent verification with disagreement resolution (additional 40 hours). The resulting two annotations yielded a Cohen’s κ \kappa of 0.932. The detailed protocol is described in Appendix B.1 .

Dataset Characteristics. For Query 1 (scRNA-seq + immunotherapy), the dataset contains: 38 papers with newly generated data meeting all criteria (Class 3), 12 papers reanalyzing existing data (Class 2), and 50 papers that fail to meet all conditions (Class 1). For Query 2 (paired scRNA-seq + scTCR-seq), papers are distributed across 8 disease categories (Classes 1–8). The per-class distribution and summary statistics can be found in Appendix B.2 (Figure 3 ). This distribution reflects realistic prevalence: newly generated data meeting stringent criteria are relatively rare, requiring substantial exploration. SciCurateBench papers average 24,318 tokens (median 21,792, IQR 15,748–31,050, range: 931–70,121), with 95% exceeding 8K tokens. Each paper comprises: (1) main manuscript (PDF parsed to text), (2) supplementary files in multiple formats: XLSX tables, CSV metadata, plain text, and (3) raw data (.mtx, .Rds, etc.). We mostly preserve raw formats to test whether agents can dynamically adapt to diverse documents, moving away from idealized, pre-curated formats that many benchmarks assume. Dataset Setup. The release format and preprocessing steps are described in Appendix B.3 .

Task 1: Science Paper Classification. Given a paper and classification guideline, determine the class label y ∈ 𝒴 y\in\mathcal{Y} where 𝒴 = { 1 , 2 , 3 } \mathcal{Y}=\{1,2,3\} for Query 1 or 𝒴 = { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 } \mathcal{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\} for Query 2. The guideline specifies conjunctive predicates that must be verified: assay type ∧ \land data novelty ∧ \land subject population ∧ \land outcome measurement ∧ \land data accessibility. For Query 1, agents must distinguish newly generated scRNA-seq data with immunotherapy response (Class 3) from reanalyzed existing data (Class 2) or irrelevant papers (Class 1). Agents receive basic file operation tools ( read_file , search_keywords , extract_citations , etc.) but must autonomously determine exploration strategies. Accuracy and F1 score are used as primary metrics. Task 2: Structured Information Retrieval. For papers classified as Class 3 in Query 1, extract structured tuples ( s i , r i ) (s_{i},r_{i}) where s i s_{i} is a sample/patient identifier and r i r_{i} is the immunotherapy response outcome. Valid response classifications include: Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria (CR, PR, SD, PD), binary labels (Responder/Non-responder), pathological responses, or survival metrics explicitly linked to immunotherapy outcomes. This task requires cross-referencing information: sample IDs may appear in one table while response data appears in another, necessitating joins across files. Agents must create custom parsing tools adapted to each paper’s unique table structure and field naming conventions. Evaluation metrics are based on Precision, Recall, and F1 for exact ( s i , r i ) (s_{i},r_{i}) matching, partial credit for correct s i s_{i} but incorrect r i r_{i} or vice versa.

Why So Difficult? In Task 1, a representative challenge arises when a paper contains some samples with the correct assay type but no associated outcome measurement, while other samples report the outcome but use a slightly different assay. The required predicates must therefore be satisfied jointly at the sample level , not merely present somewhere in the paper. Beyond addressing the practical need to curate experimental metadata, Task 2 complements the classification task in Task 1: it grounds Class 3 membership in the data itself. Many papers that look like Class 3 do not publish their full metadata, such as per-sample response labels (Appendix B.4 ). Researchers cannot know what a paper truly contains until they inspect every supplementary file and its raw data. Figure 2: Overview of LangPoli on SciCurateBench. LangPoli creates an adaptive tool based on the verbal action to interact with the environment, while ReAct chooses an action from a fixed set.

Scientific data curation can be formalized as follows. Given a paper environment E E , comprising heterogeneous files, and a task objective G G , specifying conjunctive predicates to verify, the goal is to produce a judgment J J , supported by an evidence collection V V . Traditional agent frameworks assume a fixed action space with k k actions: 𝒜 = { a 1 , a 2 , … , a k } \mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{k}\} , where each action a i a_{i} has predefined semantics (e.g., read_file(path) , search_keyword(query) ). Compared to this, LangPoli features verbal action generation : rather than selecting a t ∈ 𝒜 a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} , the framework generates natural language action descriptions a ~ t \tilde{a}_{t} that actor agents translate into paper-specific executable code c t c_{t} , effectively creating a dynamic action space 𝒜 E \mathcal{A}_{E} adapted to the environment E E . Figure 2 illustrates this distinction, where ReAct iteratively applies fixed actions and may miss crucial connections between document sections, whereas LangPoli synthesizes custom tools to navigate each paper’s unique structure.

Models and Baselines. We evaluate multiple approaches: base LLMs (GPT-4o OpenAI (2023) , Claude-3, Claude-3.5, Claude-3.7 Anthropic (2024) ), reasoning methods (CoT Wei et al. (2022) , Self-Consistency Wang et al. (2023) ), tool-based agents (ReAct Yao et al. (2023) , ChatCoT Chen et al. (2023) , LATM Cai et al. (2024) ), and feedback approaches (Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) , Self-Refine Madaan et al. (2023) ). All models are adapted to SciCurateBench. We implement two LangPoli variants: LangPoli-Basic (single actor) and LangPoli (full, MoCA). Model versions, the smaller LLMs evaluated on the public benchmarks, and the hardware are listed in Appendix D . Implementation Details. The implementations use Claude-3.5 as the base LLM unless otherwise noted. Tool creation is restricted to Python and token usage is capped at 30,000 tokens per environment. All experiments run in zero-shot without additional training. Evaluation Metrics. Paper Classification uses accuracy and F1 score, with separate reporting for Class 3 (C3), which is the class that meets all criteria in the query. In real-world scenarios, Class 3 Recall is important because even a single additional paper meeting the criteria may contain a large amount of patient data, contributing significantly to the desired data atlas. Structured Information Retrieval measures precision, recall, and accuracy for sample (patient) ID, clinical response, and their pairs. We also analyze tool effectiveness based on Maintainability Index (MI) Microsoft (2024) ; Welker (2001) . For LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC, we follow the metrics used in the original papers: Recall@K and NDCG@K.

Table 1 presents the performance of all methods on the paper classification task. Plain LLMs (GPT-4o and Claude-3.5) achieved F1 scores of only 61.00% and 58.22%, respectively. This highlights the difficulty of extracting sparse key information from long technical content. Reasoning approaches showed large improvements: CoT and Self-Con boosted F1 scores by 13.74 and 11.45 points over Claude-3.5-Sonnet, showing that conceptual task decomposition enhances information retrieval. chunks.section: 5.3 Performance on SciCurateBench: Structured Information Retrieval
chunks.text: Table 3 summarizes performance on Structured Information Retrieval. Plain LLMs are omitted as this task fundamentally requires tool usage. Tool-using agents ReAct and ChatCoT achieved reasonable F1 scores of 53.6% and 59.1%, setting performance baselines. LATM struggled due to difficulties in developing master tools for highly heterogeneous paper structures. Feedback-based agents, particularly Reflexion, demonstrated a reasonable F1 score of 57.3%, underscoring the importance of environmental interaction and self-reflection. LangPoli achieved the best results, with LangPoli (full) reaching a 69.43% F1 score (12.1 points improvement over Reflexion). From LangPoli’s strong performance, we observe the importance of an integrative design for this task where verbal feedback is transformed into actionable insights through dynamic tool creation. To understand where methods fail, we decompose errors in Appendix F.1 (Table 10 ). The dominant failure mode is missed patients: ID-only errors remain below 7% for every method, whereas missed-patient rates vary dramatically from 17.2% for LangPoli (full) to 93.8% for LATM.

chunks.section: 5.6 Variants of LangPoli Show Robust Performance
chunks.text: Table 5 presents a performance analysis of LangPoli variants. Using a single actor (LangPoli − - MoCA) decreases the F1 score by 6.46 points, highlighting the benefit of specialized parallel actors. Removing the initial exploration phase (LangPoli − - init. explore) reduces F1 by 3.60 points. Placing task guidelines early rather than late in the prompt (LangPoli − - late task guide) decreases performance by 1.86 points, a phenomenon also known as recency bias Zhao et al. (2021) . Simplified policy prompts (LangPoli − - detailed policy) reduce performance by 2.90 points, confirming the importance of prompt engineering for LLM reasoning. Simply adding self-reflection as in Reflexion (LangPoli + + reflection) decreases performance due to feedback interference , where policy agent self-reflection conflicts with critic feedback. However, replacing critic feedback with self-reflection (LangPoli − - feedback + + refl.) yields a slight improvement, suggesting opportunities for task-specific optimization. This ablation study highlights the agentic components and designs that help the task of scientific data curation.

chunks.section: 5.7 Curriculum Transfer Improves Performance on Related Tasks
chunks.text: After solving a source task G src G_{\text{src}} on a set of environments, LangPoli accumulates tool creation sequences containing verbal actions, generated code, and observations from all exploration episodes. Curriculum transfer distills this experience into generalizable strategies, combines them with the target task description into a curriculum, and instantiates the curriculum as an initial set of task-adapted tools for a related target task G tgt G_{\text{tgt}} (formalization and full results in Appendix C.3 , Table 6 ). We evaluate curriculum transfer from "scRNA-seq + immunotherapy response" to the related but distinct "scRNA-seq + scTCR-seq" classification task. While ReAct improved over the plain LLM (78.46% vs. 73.46% F1) through tool utilization, LangPoli Curriculum exhibited superior results across all curriculum lengths, reaching 87.12% accuracy and 87.55% F1 score, which is 14.09 points improvement over the baseline. Notably, even short curricula (5 iterations) performed competitively, suggesting efficient transfer of procedural knowledge between domains.

We introduce SciCurateBench, a challenging benchmark that simulates realistic scientific data curation, which we believe is the missing piece in current scientific AI agents research. SciCurateBench requires precise verification of conjunctive experimental conditions over long, heterogeneous documents (manuscript, supplementary files, and raw data). Our experiments show that this task is difficult, even for advanced LLMs and popular agents, and that the primary failure mode is the inability to identify key evidence buried in supplementary files. To study what closes this gap, we propose LangPoli, a multi-agent framework that adapts established agentic components to scientific data curation by decoupling a natural-language policy from per-document code synthesis. LangPoli shows strong performance on both benchmark tasks, transfers to public re-ranking benchmarks, and, through curriculum transfer, adapts to a related task within a few iterations.

Several limitations should be noted. First, SciCurateBench currently contains 200 papers. Although its total content volume substantially exceeds that of many existing benchmarks, scale expansion is an important direction for future work. Second, the current benchmark focuses on life science research, and extending it to additional scientific domains remains an important direction. Third, LangPoli depends on capable base models, since it must generate goal-oriented, error-free code. The scope of our work is to address the important yet underexplored task of scientific data curation with a new benchmark dataset and to provide baseline methods. Although each component of LangPoli is based on established agentic AI works, we believe its integrative design yields meaningful insights into the problem. Future work may evaluate more recent methods in agentic programming and RAG.

LLM reasoning. Recent advances have enhanced LLM reasoning through structured prompting and tool integration. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Wei et al. (2022) decomposes complex problems into sequential sub-steps. ReAct Yao et al. (2023) pioneered cyclical interleaving of reasoning, action, and observation, while ChatCoT Chen et al. (2023) showed that conversational formats improve tool interaction. Feedback-based refinement has further advanced reasoning capabilities: Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) employs explicit verbal feedback across multiple cycles, and SelfRefine Madaan et al. (2023) uses internal correction loops. More recently, Agent-as-a-Judge Zhuge et al. (2025) uses agentic systems to evaluate other agentic systems and provide intermediate feedback throughout the task-solving process, and DPSDP Yuan and Xie (2025) trains an actor-critic pair of LLMs with reinforcement learning to iteratively refine answers. We thus note that general verbal feedback is an established concept in the field and point the readers to a survey Liu et al. (2025) for more related works. Our work studies the effectiveness of verbal info-gap feedback within the scope of scientific data curation.

Tool creation. A separate line of work explores tool creation. LATM Cai et al. (2024) creates generalized tools for problem classes, though this approach falters when "master tools" are impractical to construct. CodeAct Wang et al. (2024b) generates code as actions instead of relying on the fixed JSON format, thereby revising prior actions or emitting new ones upon new observations. ToolMaker Wölflein et al. (2025) takes a task description and a link to a code repository, and generates code to turn the repository into an LLM-compatible tool. DynaSaur Nguyen et al. (2025) lets an agent create new actions as needed by writing and executing programs, and accumulates the generated actions for reuse in later tasks. LangPoli is structurally close to these methods but decouples policy (guidelines) from environment-specific implementation (code).

Scientific AI agents. Recent works have begun applying LLM agents to scientific workflows. ChemCrow M. Bran et al. (2024) integrates expert-designed chemistry tools for synthesis planning and execution, including direct interaction with a robotic synthesis platform. The AI Scientist Lu et al. (2024) demonstrates end-to-end automation of machine learning research, from hypothesis generation to paper writing. BixBench Mitchener et al. (2025) is a benchmark dataset comprising 60 real-world bioinformatics analysis scenarios with 200 open-ended queries. ScienceAgentBench Chen et al. (2024) evaluates agentic systems on data-driven scientific discovery tasks, such as “Train a cell counting model on the BBBC002 datasets Carpenter et al. (2006) " or “Train a multitask model on the Clintox dataset Wu et al. (2018) to predict a drug’s toxicity and FDA approval status". Existing research on scientific AI agents predominantly targets downstream scientific tasks of hypothesis generation, experimental design, data analysis. It is typically assumed that curated input data is already available. We think the upstream bottleneck of curating experimental data from raw literature remains underexplored.

Three domain experts with a life science background (3–12 years experience) performed annotation. The annotation process involved: (1) examining full manuscripts, supplementary materials, and hosted data to verify experimental assay types, (2) determining whether data were newly generated or reanalyzed from prior publications, (3) validating clinical outcome availability, and (4) extracting structured metadata (sample/patient identifiers and response information). Annotations were conducted in two stages: primary annotation (160 hours) followed by independent verification with disagreement resolution (additional 40 hours). The senior annotator’s labels were merged into the final consensus through joint discussion. The resulting two annotations yielded a Cohen’s κ \kappa of 0.932. Discrepancies arose primarily from ambiguous data provenance statements and unstandardized naming conventions (e.g., “sample ID” vs “patient ID” vs “donor ID”). Approximately 10% of annotations required discussion and joint re-examination to reach consensus.

For Query 2 (paired scRNA-seq + scTCR-seq), papers are distributed across 8 disease categories: healthy controls (Class 2, n = 6 n=6 ), infections excluding COVID-19 (Class 3, n = 6 n=6 ), COVID-19 (Class 4, n = 11 n=11 ), inflammation (Class 5, n = 10 n=10 ), immune-related adverse events (Class 6, n = 2 n=2 ), solid tumors (Class 7, n = 30 n=30 ), other conditions (Class 8, n = 6 n=6 ), and no qualifying data (Class 1, n = 30 n=30 ). Summary statistics can be found in Figure 3 . Figure 3: SciCurateBench dataset statistics: (a) journal distribution, (b) publication years, (c) class distributions for both queries

The download links to all materials for each paper, including manuscripts, supplementary files, and hosted data, are included in the release. These links typically require journal website access permission. To comply with copyright restrictions, users should manually download files through a web browser. The preprocessing script converts the downloaded materials into formats suitable for experimental use. Classification labels are provided in separate CSV files, while Structured Information Retrieval labels are supplied in a PKL file. We convert all PDF files to plain text using the Python PyMuPDF package Artifex Software, Inc. (2026) . For XLSX files, we separate individual sheets and convert them to text files. We chose text format over CSV because many supplementary tables contain complex structures that are difficult to parse. We also annotated key files containing critical information (e.g., sample/patient IDs and immunotherapy response rates).

chunks.section: B.4 Why Class 3 Membership Is Hard to Verify
chunks.text: Many papers that look like Class 3 do not publish their full metadata (such as per-sample response labels) for diverse reasons. Some release their assay data but withhold clinical outcomes as proprietary. Others report only aggregate demographics rather than individual-level metadata. In some cases, the patient-level information resides only in the hosted raw data, which is exactly what makes manual curation so time-consuming.

chunks.section: Appendix E Results on Public Datasets: LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC
chunks.text: To show the generality of the proposed method on literature curation, we benchmark LangPoli on the re-ranking task of three publicly available datasets: LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. The re-ranking task asks the system to re-rank the top candidates, retrieved by the base method such as BM25, to determine the final permutation. We observe that LangPoli outperforms the strong RankGPT baseline (Table 4 ). Improvements are clearer when the underlying retrieval method is simpler (e.g., BM25 compared to GritLM), suggesting that LangPoli effectively compensates for weaker initial retrieval while still providing gains on top of neural retrievers. Table 7 shows LangPoli improves performance compared to the baseline BM25 and RankGPT across query sources and paper venues. Table 8 reports re-ranking performance on three BEIR subsets (Touche, News, and Robust04) that have the longest document contexts in the dataset (640.24, 1123.73, and 806.84 average words, respectively). Across a diverse set of base LLMs, LangPoli consistently matches or outperforms RankGPT on most dataset–model combinations. Table 9 shows that LangPoli with GPT-4o-mini consistently outperforms RankGPT using the same base model. Overall, these results show that LangPoli generalizes beyond life science domain. More importantly, building on established agentic components, our integrative design benefits literature curation and information retrieval tasks.
